conventions.rule: The name Caesar denotes several men: the dictator, his adopted heir (the in-scope Augustus) both before and after he took that title, Tiberius, and the young grandson Gaius, among others. Decide from context each time; for the battle and its build-up it normally means Augustus, not Julius Caesar.
conventions.why: The Augustus aliases and the Julius Caesar label both match Caesar, and the source also applies it to Tiberius and Gaius.

evidence.quotation: The command of the right wing of Caesar's fleet was entrusted to Marcus Lurius
Caesar was only about eighteen years of age at the time of Sulla's dictator­ship
On hearing of this disaster, Caesar flew to his father's side.
Shortly after this Gaius Caesar, who had previously made a tour of other provinces

conventions.rule: Pompey and Pompeius can mean Pompeius Magnus or his son Sextus Pompey, and Antonius can mean Mark Antony or his brothers Lucius and Gaius or his son Iulus; Marcus Agrippa can also mean Agrippa's posthumous son. Identify each from context before linking to an in-scope person.
conventions.why: Shared family names would otherwise be linked to the wrong in-scope person.

evidence.quotation: Pompey lost almost all his ships, and fled to Asia
Antonius, beaten on all sides by the forces of Caesar, had taken refuge in Perusia
Marcus Agrippa, to whom Julia had given birth after the death of Agrippa

conventions.rule: The source spells the in-scope Lucius Gellius Poplicola as Publicola, and names several different men Gnaeus Domitius; link only the one who deserts Antony before the battle to Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus.
conventions.why: Spelling variant not among aliases, and the Domitii are distinct generations.

evidence.quotation: The command of Antony's fleet was entrusted to Publicola and Sosius.
Gnaeus Domitius, father of Lucius Domitius our late contemporary
In this year Gnaeus Domitius, the tribune of the people, passed a law

conventions.rule: Years are given by the pair of consuls in office, or as a count of years back from the author's own day (the consulship of his addressee Vinicius), or by founding of the city. Keep these expressions as the time expression; add a year only when the passage itself states one.
conventions.why: Consular and relative datings are not plain years and depend on the author's present.

evidence.quotation: Then, in the consul­ship of Caesar and Messala Corvinus, the decisive battle took place at Actium.
One hundred and twenty years ago, in the consul­ship of Lucius Caesar and Publius Rutilius

conventions.rule: The author is an openly partisan admirer of Augustus and Tiberius and hostile to Antony and Cleopatra; his moral verdicts, his claim that the outcome was settled before the fighting, and his inferences about what Antony or Augustus would have done are his judgments, so draft them as interpretation, not as events.
conventions.why: Evaluative and counterfactual statements are woven into the narrative.

evidence.quotation: The victory of the Caesarian party was a certainty long before the battle.
one might question whether in case of victory he would have acted according to Cleopatra's will or his own
it may be inferred how moderate a use Caesar would have made of the victory

conventions.rule: Quoted remarks and reported shouting, and the author's own direct addresses to a character or to his patron, are rhetoric; draft only the fact that the utterance was made, not its content as narrative fact.
conventions.why: The author apostrophises figures and reports pointed sayings.

evidence.quotation: But you accomplished nothing, Mark Antony
My services to Antony are too great, and his kindness to me too well known
kept shouting and pointing out to them that Antony had fled

conventions.rule: A small bullet mark before a word is a transcriber's marker for an editorial note, not part of the text; ignore it.
conventions.why: Markers are embedded in the passage text.

notes: Velleius is a near-contemporary officer under Tiberius writing a compressed, panegyrical survey; the battle narrative is brief and framed by pre-battle desertions and command assignments. He often cross-refers to his own earlier narrative, which signals no new event.
